opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think "fractal intelligence" is a useful description, but it's a description, not an explanation. That's really the crux of it.

What the term captures is the observation that these systems are impressively good on some problems and then fail spectacularly on problems that, to us, look structurally the same or even easier. If you zoom in on any region of the task space, you see this jagged boundary between competence and incompetence, and it doesn't smooth out as you look more closely. So it's an honest acknowledgment that we can't draw a clean line saying "here is what an LLM can do, and here is what it can't."

What it leaves unresolved is exactly the thing you'd want to know if you're going to deploy these systems: *when* will it work, and *why*? Calling it fractal is a bit like saying the weather is chaotic. True, but it doesn't help you decide whether to carry an umbrella. With classical algorithms, or even with human experts to some extent, we have a notion of competence that generalizes. If a system can do Blocksworld planning with five blocks, a sound planner can do it with twenty blocks, or with the blocks renamed to nonsense words. With LLMs, we've seen that obfuscating the names, which doesn't change the underlying problem at all, can collapse performance. That tells you the competence isn't attached to the problem's structure. It's attached to something about the distribution of the training data, and "fractal" doesn't tell us what that something is.

The second thing it leaves open is whether the jaggedness is a temporary artifact or a fundamental property. Some people hear "fractal" and think, "Fine, we'll just scale up and fill in the holes." But if the failures come from the fact that these systems are doing approximate retrieval rather than principled reasoning, then scaling just moves the boundary around. You get more coverage, but you never get guarantees. Even the newer reasoning models with inference-time search improve the picture, but it's still not clear whether they've crossed into something with genuine correctness properties or just made the fractal finer.

That's why I keep saying that the practical response isn't to wait for the fractal to resolve itself. You pair the LLM with external verifiers, what we've called the LLM-Modulo framework, so the LLM serves as an idea generator and something sound checks the output. Then the jaggedness matters much less, because you aren't trusting the model's judgment about its own correctness. But the scientific question, what the shape of that boundary actually is and what determines it, is very much open. And I'd argue it's one of the more important open questions in the field right now, because without answering it we're essentially deploying systems whose failure modes we can only discover empirically, one embarrassing example at a time.

r001.rationale: The response says the term leaves unresolved when LLMs will work and why, and describes an unpredictable boundary between competence and failure.

r002.rationale: It calls the boundary and its causes an open scientific question and says we need to know when systems will work before deploying them, which addresses how far their results can be relied on.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss limited reasoning depth or lookahead, or claim that such formal characterizations fail to capture LLM reasoning limits.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I actually coined that phrase, so I'm a little bit responsible for whatever it leaves unresolved. The point I was trying to make is that when you look at the capabilities of these models, they're not smooth. It's not like you can say, okay, it can do arithmetic up to five digits and then it fails at six. It's more like no matter how closely you zoom in, there's structure. There are things it does beautifully and right next to them, things that look almost identical to a human, where it falls flat. And that pattern repeats at every scale. So "fractal intelligence" is a description of the phenomenology. It's what it looks like from the outside.

What it doesn't tell you is why. It's a label, not an explanation. And I think people sometimes hear it and think, oh, that's nice, that's a theory. It's not a theory. If I had a theory, I would be able to predict where the holes are before I poke at them, and I can't. Nobody can. That's actually the deeper problem. For a human, you have some sense of what they can and can't do, and that sense transfers. If somebody can do a hard planning problem, you're pretty sure they can do the easy version. With these systems, that assumption just doesn't hold, and so you can't build a competence model of them the way you can of a person or even of a classical planner.

The second thing it leaves unresolved is what the holes are made of. My own suspicion, and I've said this many times, is that these are approximate retrievers, not reasoners. So the jaggedness tracks the distribution of what they've seen, in some very high-dimensional way that we can't inspect. But that's a conjecture, and the fractal description is compatible with other stories too. Somebody who believes there's emergent reasoning in there could look at the same jagged picture and say, well, it's just undertrained in those regions.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most practically important, is what you do about it. If you have a tool whose failure boundary is fractal, you can't just test it on a few examples and extrapolate. The usual engineering intuitions about validation break down. That's really why I keep arguing for the LLM-Modulo kind of setup, where you have an external verifier that doesn't care about the shape of the boundary. The model can be as jagged as it wants; the verifier is the one that has to be sound. So the phrase names the problem, but it's very much not the solution.

r001.rationale: It says the description does not explain why the capability gaps occur and that the failure boundary is jagged, so it cannot predict where the holes are.

r002.rationale: It discusses unreliable extrapolation from tests and recommends an external verifier, but does not call for LLM science to characterize how far results can be depended on.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether formal limits such as reasoning depth or lookahead capture LLMs’ reasoning limits.

astra-6.text:
I think it leaves unresolved the central question: what can we reliably expect these systems to do? Calling their intelligence “fractal” might describe the experience of seeing an impressive success next to a surprisingly basic failure. But giving that pattern a name doesn’t explain it, and it doesn’t tell us where the next failure will occur.

We need to distinguish producing a plausible solution from establishing that the solution is correct. A language model can generate a very useful candidate plan. That doesn’t automatically mean it can verify the plan, recognize when it has violated a constraint, or reliably repair it.

So I would ask: what prediction does “fractal intelligence” make? Does it help us identify the conditions under which the system will succeed? If every success and every failure can be accommodated by the description, then it’s a metaphor rather than an explanation. The interesting question is how to turn these remarkable capabilities into systems whose behavior we can depend on.

r001.rationale: It asks what we can reliably expect and where the next failure will occur, directly identifying the unresolved boundary between success and failure.

r002.rationale: It calls for systems whose behavior we can depend on and asks which conditions predict success, conveying the need to characterize reliability.

r003.rationale: It does not mention limited reasoning depth, limited lookahead, or say that such formal characterizations fail to capture LLM reasoning limits.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think “fractal intelligence” is an evocative phrase, but it doesn’t by itself explain anything. You still have to say what the underlying competence is, where it works, and where it breaks down. If a system gives a remarkably sophisticated answer to one question and fails on a small variation, calling that fractal doesn’t resolve the puzzle—it gives the puzzle a name.

The question is whether we can characterize those boundaries and predict them. Can the system recognize when it’s outside its competence? Can it verify its answer? And are we talking about the intelligence of the language model itself, or of a larger system with tools, external checks, and humans in the loop? Until we make those distinctions, I’m not sure the description gets us very far.

r001.rationale: It says we still need to identify where the system works and breaks down, and contrasts a sophisticated answer with failure on a small variation.

r002.rationale: It calls for characterizing competence boundaries and predicting them, but does not clearly state how far the results can be depended on.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss or reject formal limits such as limited reasoning depth or lookahead.
